SURGO × UNIVERSITY OF MANITOBA · CÔTE D’IVOIRE

Demand, services and modern contraceptive use

Department-wide supply assignment. Each woman receives the recorded facility averages for her own department-equivalent area. Demand indicators remain personal; Rural/Urban residence remains a model covariate.

Joint evidence helps identify where reported concerns coincide with service weaknesses. Associations and relative planning categories do not establish causal binding constraints or budget allocations.

02 · USE, INTENTION AND METHOD CHOICE

Among women SURGO classifies as in need of family planning

From this section onward: original FPN2 = 1, with consent and WEIGHT, gives 4,292 women. No historical need_n reconstruction or permanent-protection additions are applied.

All bars use 4,292 women in need as the denominator; subgroups overlap. Percentages use WEIGHT; n is unweighted. Capped whiskers use recorded IDZD census-district clusters, with the need subgroup selected after constructing the full consenting positive-weight design. Original strata and FPC are unavailable. Preference concerns the wanted method at initiation; intention concerns any method without a specified future initiation window.

Initial pattern. Current use is 71.2%, including 57.0% modern use. Nonusers with intention account for 11.4%, and nonusers without stated intention 17.2%. These are concurrent groups, not observed transitions.

Supply measurement qualification. Popular-product stock is undefined for 55.1% of linked facilities, with applicability and upstream coding limitations identified. Original indicators are retained for comparison with Friday; stock-related scores and associations are provisional pending source review. Unknowns are not coded zero. See the stock appendix.
Main score and classification
  1. Calculate six concern prevalences using valid-domain answers and WEIGHT; average each original facility indicator over valid facilities in the department.
  2. Standardize each component: subtract its mean across valid departments and divide by its sample SD. Departments contribute equally to the reference.
  3. Average six standardized components separately on each side. A missing component prevents a complete score. Higher demand means more concern; higher favorable supply means stronger provision.
  4. Flag demand strictly above -0.017469; favorable supply strictly below -0.012715. Ties are unflagged; supply risk is negative readiness.

Demand has 82 reference areas; complete supply scores exist for 77. The four unmatched areas and Daoukro’s undefined free provision remain supply-unassessed. Categories are relative planning signals.

Both: 21Demand only: 18Supply only: 17Neither flagged: 21Supply unassessed: 5

Planning signal. 21 areas have both sides flagged, 18 demand only, 17 supply only, 21 neither and 5 supply-unassessed. Investigate component priorities and response coverage before selecting an intervention.

Which priorities recur across departments?

Count how often each component appears among a department’s three priorities: the lowest standardized provision components for supply, and the highest standardized concern components for demand. These are counts of departments, not percentages of women or estimated causes of nonuse.

Both-flagged departments are excluded from these two group summaries. A department contributes to three components, so percentages do not sum to 100%. These are relative priorities, not service-standard failures. Popular-product stock remains provisional because of the missingness and original coding limitations documented in the appendix.

Short- and long-acting options together means at least one long-acting and three short-acting categories at the same facility. Free provision and training average within-facility proportions; they are not shares of facilities offering any free product or having any trained provider. The confidence indicator is unchanged: it measures confidence choosing a method or managing side effects, not objective knowledge.

04 · ADJUSTED ASSOCIATIONS
Supply measurement qualification. Popular-product stock is undefined for 55.1% of linked facilities, with applicability and upstream coding limitations identified. Original indicators are retained for comparison with Friday; stock-related scores and associations are provisional pending source review. Unknowns are not coded zero. See the stock appendix.

Modern use in relation to personal concerns and local services

All models: 3,854 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,211 modern users across 77 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

Score assigned to each womanConstructionObserved model variation
Demand risk scoreStandardize her own six demand responses using weighted item means and population SDs among valid FPN2 = 1 women; average all six. Her department or residence does not determine this score.62 distinct values across 3,854 women.
Supply risk scoreStandardize her assigned six department-wide measures against the valid department planning means/SDs. Average and reverse the sign: higher = weaker provision.77 distinct numeric scores across 77 department-equivalent areas; no geographic fallback is applied.
ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.37 (0.28–0.49) and the supply score odds ratio 0.92 (0.69–1.22) per one original average-z index point. These are adjusted associations on the same women. Read the intervals against 1 and consult the joint tests below; overlap with 1 means the direction is not resolved at that confidence level. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.16 (0.08–0.29); health beliefs have OR 0.67 (0.53–0.84); low method confidence has OR 0.67 (0.53–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.578 with only 0.93 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so that block test is particularly weak. Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -39.9 percentage points for opposition and -8.4 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

Interpret this item cautiously. Healthcare permission barriers have OR 1.31 (1.07–1.59) and an adjusted difference of +5.3 points. This does not mean restrictions improve use: the item concerns general healthcare permission, and confounding, selection and reverse direction remain possible.

Each joint model has two tests. Demand tests its one score coefficient or all six concern coefficients together; supply tests its one score coefficient. Holm correction applies within those two tests per model. These tests do not establish whether demand matters more than supply, equality between them, or causal binding constraints.

DEFINITIONS AND VERIFICATION

Measures, denominators and interpretation

Demand domains and unknown responses
DomainQuestion and coding
Healthcare permission barriersHS7C: 1 = permission to see a doctor is a challenge; 2 = no. General healthcare permission, not FP-specific partner approval.
Anticipated social stigmaPB7B/C: 1/2 on either item about being seen or what others would say. Zero requires both valid 3/4 responses.
Health / side-effect beliefsPB2A–C: 1/2 on any item about health problems, reduced sexual desire or babies with birth defects. Zero requires all valid 3/4 responses. Bleeding and later fertility are excluded. Beliefs are not personally experienced side effects.
Future-fertility concernsMP4_a–f reversible-method concerns, requiring coherent MP4_a–i 0/1 selections, no none-plus-method contradiction, an explicit selection or none, and MP4_99 = 0. Sterilization items MP4_g/h do not create a concern.
Low method knowledge · retained labelMC5A/B: low confidence choosing a suitable method or handling side effects/switching (3/4 on either). This is confidence/self-efficacy, not objective knowledge. Zero requires both valid 1/2 answers.
Opposes family planningFP1: against (3/4) versus in favor (1/2). Unfamiliarity (5), no opinion (99) and other special responses remain unresolved.

A known positive establishes an any-concern flag; zero requires valid negatives on every included item. Remaining combinations stay unresolved. These questions are not restricted to married women or nonusers. The retained knowledge label measures subjective confidence.

Supply definitions and response coverage
MeasureCalculation and interpretation
Short + long-acting offeringMean of UoM one_larc_3_sa_offer, joined as share_offer_larc_and_3_sa: share meeting the original ≥1 long-acting plus ≥3 short-acting product/category rule.
Free-product provisionMean of valid facility p_free_prod, joined as mean_p_free_prod. A value of 60% means the average reporting facility provides 60% of its recorded products free; not that 60% of facilities offer any free method.
Trained-provider shareMean of valid facility p_train proportions, using original UoM personnel/topic eligibility. Not the percentage of facilities with at least one trained provider.
FP counselor availabilitys7_2: Yes/(Yes+No); 1 = Yes, 2 = No, unknown/special responses excluded. Availability is not counseling receipt or quality.
At least one LARC in stockMean of one_larc_stockin, joined as share_stocked_1plus_larc. The country-wide three-LARC indicator is constant FALSE and cannot be standardized; this existing joined alternative is explicitly used.
Most-popular product in stockn_mp_in_stock_true/(true+false), among facilities with known status. Each facility refers to its own most-popular product, not the woman’s preferred method.

Valid zero/FALSE values are included; unknown and undefined values are excluded from each measure’s denominator. Within-facility proportions are averaged equally, rather than replaced by pooled product/personnel ratios. Counseling is retained: 2,011 Yes, 378 No and 323 Not applicable among 2,712 linked facilities. Not applicable is not a blank or an automatic No.

Survey design, adjustment and model sample

All models use original WEIGHT and department-clustered CR2 covariance with Satterthwaite intervals. Recorded IDZD census districts support overview intervals and an inference sensitivity; original strata/FPC are unavailable. Adjust for age, age², education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. No random effects or interactions are fitted.

The model comparison uses 3,854 women, including 2,211 modern users. The overview retains all 4,292 women in need. Department supply is complete for 4,200; 92 lack a complete profile. Models additionally require known demand, outcome and covariates. Friday’s residence-specific models used 3,768 women; this department-wide version uses 3,854. Differences between those reports reflect both exposure resolution and sample composition, not the aggregation change alone.

The upstream CDI selection matches lettered s6_16a–i questions and excludes unlettered s6_16, the male-condom stock question. All 262 facilities identifying male condoms as most popular therefore lack this derived flag. Also, any(present) without removing unknown brand values returns unknown when no brand is known present and at least one is inapplicable. Some procedure or behavior methods have no comparable commodity-stock item.

Among the 1,493 undefined flags, 1,153 facilities report FP services, 323 report No and 17 have another/unknown answer. Undefined does not justify coding all as not offering methods or out of stock. “No popular product identified” is a ranking result, not proof of no demand.

Original indicators are preserved for replication. No coding repair is silently introduced. Stock-related scores and model associations require reviewed source correction before use as firm evidence of service shortfalls. The omitted-question limitation requires source review; restricting records cannot recover an excluded input question.

APPENDIX C · PCA AND MODEL ROBUSTNESS

Alternative scores from the same personal and department inputs

Separate weighted PCAs use six personal demand and six department supply components, including counseling. Demand PCA uses 3,954 women; supply uses 4,200 women across 77 complete department profiles, weighted by represented women’s summed WEIGHT.

Interpretation. Demand PC1 captures 27.3% of input variation; supply PC1 45.4%. Supply PC1 has mixed signs: training and popular-stock load negatively. Its negative is a pattern score, not uniformly worse provision. Coefficients describe input variation, not causal effects or investment priorities.

The same five modern-use models using PCA scores

All models: 3,854 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,211 modern users across 77 departments. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, department-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.64 (0.58–0.70) and the supply score odds ratio 0.95 (0.86–1.05) per one oriented PC1 unit. These are adjusted associations on the same women. Read the intervals against 1 and consult the joint tests below; overlap with 1 means the direction is not resolved at that confidence level. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.16 (0.09–0.29); health beliefs have OR 0.67 (0.53–0.84); low method confidence has OR 0.67 (0.53–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.542 with only 0.92 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so that block test is particularly weak. Use the heatmap to locate these concerns alongside service weaknesses; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

What this means for planning. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -39.7 percentage points for opposition and -8.3 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps identify patterns to investigate; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

PCA interpretation. Supply PC1 has negative coefficients for trained-provider share and popular-product stock, alongside positive coefficients for other provision measures. Its negative is labeled a supply pattern score. It is not a monotonic supply-risk index, and its association cannot be interpreted as the effect of worsening every service domain.

Geographic leverage and uncertainty

Unequal department contributions mean nominal geographic count does not guarantee precise inference. The six-indicator demand block can have fewer than one effective denominator degree of freedom under CR2 testing. Its weak joint test does not establish no demand role or invalidate every pointwise association.
